title: Jenna Ortega Says She Hopes ‘Klara and the Sun’ Encourages People to ‘Put Down the Computers and Phones’ as Dystopian Film World Premieres in London
description: Jenna Ortega hopes that her new film, the dystopian sci-fi “Klara and the Sun,” can remind people to live in the moment in the age of AI and all-co
body:
Jenna Ortega hopes that her new film, the dystopian sci-fi “Klara and the Sun,” can remind people to live in the moment in the age of AI and all-consuming technology. 

	“I think we gotta put our focus on one another and put down the computers and phones,” the star told Variety on the red carpet at the movie’s world premiere at London Film Festival on Thursday night.

	Ortega, wearing a stunning yellow lace dress and hair piece, added: “Remember to be present and to appreciate people while they’re standing right in front of you.”
	

	Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s bestselling 2021 novel of the same name, “Klara and the Sun” is set in a future where advances in genetic engineering have divided humans into strict social classes. Ortega plays Klara, an artificial android companion who is purchased for an ailing girl named Josie (Mia Tharia). “Klara and the Sun” is directed by “Thor” helmer Taika Waititi and also stars Amy Adams as Josie’s mother, Aran Murphy (son of Cillian Murphy), Natasha Lyonne, Steve Buscemi and more.


	Waititi, Adams, Murphy and Lyonne all walked the London Film Festival red carpet on Thursday night, alongside Waititi’s wife Rita Ora and a surprise appearance from Florence Pugh, who stunned in a blue floral gown with statement sleeves. Pugh enthusiastically greeted Ortega and Adams before they all posed for photos together alongside producer Rachel Forman.



	

					Florence Pugh, Amy Adams, Jenna Ortega and Rachel Forman at the “Klara and the Sun” world premiere in London.
									Getty Images for BFI
	



	Standing alongside Ortega, Adams added that everyone she’s spoken to has gotten “something different” out of the film. “That, to me, is a really successful film that communicates something different to each viewer. So I like hearing what people get out of it,” she said.
	

	Ortega clarified that though Klara is an “artificial friend,” she doesn’t work like the AI that we know today.

	“AI I guess pulls all this information from the internet and Klara gets all her information from the real world,” she said. “So that’s a little bit different. She’s kind of like a toddler in a sense. Playing her specifically in this film was really interesting because Taika wanted a more human approach, so he didn’t want to do movement that was too robotic, maybe more sort of clumsy and unknowing.”

	“Klara and the Sun” is set to hit theaters via Sony Pictures on Oct. 23.

schema.headline: Jenna Ortega Says She Hopes ‘Klara and the Sun’ Encourages People to ‘Put Down the Computers and Phones’ as Dystopian Film World Premieres in London

title: Steven Soderbergh to Help Finish ‘The Batman 2’ Filming After Matt Reeves Stepped Away for Family Matter
description: Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to help complete “The Batman Part II” while director Matt Reeves is on hiatus dealing with a personal matter, Vari
body:
Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to help complete “The Batman Part II” while director Matt Reeves is on hiatus dealing with a personal matter, Variety has confirmed.

	“As Matt Reeves continues to attend to an ongoing family matter, Steven Soderbergh, as an admirer of Matt’s work, approached Matt and will step in, with the full support of DC Studios, to help the writer-director complete the final weeks of principal photography on ‘The Batman Part 2,'” a studio rep said in a statement. “Matt and Steven will work closely together with the actors and crew to fulfill Matt’s vision of the film.”
	

	Soderbergh said in his own statement, “I thought Matt Reeves’ work on ‘The Batman’ was stunning; it was intentional, specific and rigorously coherent. The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.” 


	Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced “The Batman Part II” production pause in early October, stating that Reeves temporarily stepped away from the project to handle a “family matter.” 

	“Production on ‘The Batman Part II’ has been temporarily paused while Matt Reeves focuses on a family matter,” a rep said in a statement at the time. “Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon.”

	The highly anticipated “Batman” sequel has experienced several delays since it was announced at CinemaCon 2022. The original release date was set for Oct. 2, 2026, before Warner Bros. delayed it to Oct. 1, 2027. In June, the film was pushed again to February 2028. Reeves’ first “Batman” was released in March 2022.
	

	Robert Pattinson returns as the Caped Crusader in “The Batman Part II.” Other cast members include Scarlett Johansson, Colin Farrell, Sebastian Stan, Andy Serkis and Jeffrey Wright.

schema.headline: Steven Soderbergh to Help Finish ‘The Batman 2’ Filming After Matt Reeves Stepped Away for Family Matter

title: Denis Villeneuve Chose to Direct New James Bond Movie After ‘Dune 3’ Because ‘I Need a Powerful Rocket to Pull Me Away From Arrakis’
description: Denis Villeneuve recently told Empire that he returned to “Dune” for a third and final chapter so he can be “severe with the material,” and that hi
body:
Denis Villeneuve recently told Empire that he returned to “Dune” for a third and final chapter so he can be “severe with the material,” and that his upcoming James Bond movie will be the “very powerful rocket” he needs to “pull me away from Arrakis.” 

	“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite — I’m tired of it.’ I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he explained. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”
	

	Villeneuve, director of “Prisoners,” “Sicario” and “Arrival,” has not helmed a film outside the “Dune” franchise since “Part One” was released in 2021. “Dune: Part Two” hit theaters in 2024, and “Dune: Part Three” will debut on Dec. 18, 2026. 


	In June 2025, it was revealed that Villeneuve, a self-described “die-hard Bond fan,” will direct the next 007 movie. There’s been much speculation about who will take up the mantle after Daniel Craig’s 15-year run. Gary Oldman recently claimed that the next James Bond has already been picked, but no official casting announcement has been made. 

	Based on Frank Herbert’s “Dune Messiah,” “Dune: Part Three” chronicles Paul Atreides’ fall from prophetic liberator to tyrannical emperor. Timothée Chalamet stars as Paul alongside Zendaya, Jason Momoa, Florence Pugh, Robert Pattinson, Anya Taylor-Joy, Rebecca Ferguson, Josh Brolin and Javier Bardem. 
	

	In her own sit-down with Empire, Zendaya discussed the arc of her character, Chani, in “Dune: Part 3.” She revealed that in the new film, Chani feels “a deep pain” and “a deep betrayal” as Paul becomes unrecognizable from the man she fell in love with. 

	“In the previous film, she opened herself up to the idea of letting someone in, allowing a space for love or gentleness,” she said. “Well, we see how that goes. That part of her life is not as present anymore.”

schema.headline: Denis Villeneuve Chose to Direct New James Bond Movie After ‘Dune 3’ Because ‘I Need a Powerful Rocket to Pull Me Away From Arrakis’

title: ‘Fourth Wing’ TV Series Casts Emilio Sakraya as Xaden Riorson
description:
Attention, “Fourth Wing” cadets: Amazon Prime Video’s TV adaptation of Rebecca Yarros’ bestselling romantasy series has found your wing leader.

	E
body:
Attention, “Fourth Wing” cadets: Amazon Prime Video’s TV adaptation of Rebecca Yarros’ bestselling romantasy series has found your wing leader.

	Emilio Sakraya has been cast in the role of Xaden Riorson, Variety has learned. He will star opposite Esther McGregor (“We Were Liars”) as Violet Sorrengail on the Prime Video TV series. Amazon declined comment.

	Sakraya has a hefty list of credits in both TV and film from his native Germany as well as in the U.S.; his credits include “Rhinegold,” “Tribes of Europa” and “Warrior Nun.” His other recent projects include “Those About to Die,” and he’s set to appear in Season 3 of “One Piece.”
	

	“Fourth Wing” is set inside the brutal world of Basgiath War College, where there is only one rule: graduate or die. Twenty-year-old Violet Sorrengail was always expected to live a quiet life — but she’s sent on an entirely different path when her mother, a general in the military, orders her to join the hundreds of candidates striving to become dragon riders, the elite of Navarre.


	Starting with the release of New York Times bestseller “Fourth Wing” in May 2023, Yarros’ “The Empyrean” book series currently includes sequels “Iron Flame” (November 2023) and “Onyx Storm” (January 2025.) This September, Yarros released the novella “Threshing Day,” which tells 13 stories set in the “The Empyrean” universe. The titles and release dates for the planned fourth and fifth books have yet to be announced.

	Ordered to series at Amazon in May, Meredith Averill (“Anne With an E”) is showrunner and executive producer of “Fourth Wing.” The show is also executive produced by Kilter Films (Lisa Joy — who also directs the pilot, Jonathan Nolan and Athena Wickham), Outlier Society (Michael B. Jordan and Elizabeth Raposo) and Premeditated Productions (Liz Pelletier and Sherryl Clark).

schema.headline: ‘Fourth Wing’ TV Series Casts Emilio Sakraya as Xaden Riorson

title: Skydance’s Market Value Is Currently Less Than Half What Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Combined Were Worth
description:
David Ellison’s freshly formed Skydance Corp. is off to a rocky start on Wall Street. 

	He won Warner Bros. Discovery after a yearlong battle. But
body:
David Ellison’s freshly formed Skydance Corp. is off to a rocky start on Wall Street. 

	He won Warner Bros. Discovery after a yearlong battle. But investors, at this point, appear to believe he wildly overpaid for the deal — that the newly merged company, dubbed Skydance Corp., is worth nowhere near the $78 billion in cash Paramount shelled out for WBD.

	As of Oct. 5, the last day of trading for WBD and Paramount Skydance (PSKY) on Nasdaq, Warner Bros. Discovery had a market capitalization of $77.7 billion and Paramount was around $11 billion. Today, Skydance has a market cap of under $40 billion — less than half the predecessor companies’ combined value.
	

	On Wednesday, Skydance’s stock plunged 22%. That came after the company distributed about 471 million warrants giving holders of Paramount Skydance’s PSKY Class B shares the option to purchase stock in the new company for $12/share.

	What happened? On Tuesday after the market close, the New York Stock Exchange made a technical adjustment to Skydance’s share price, reducing it by 19.4 cents, to account for the issuance of the warrants (trading on NYSE as “SKYD.WS”). The speculation is that index funds sold off the warrants they held when those start trading; that, in turn, was interpreted as a sell-off event by automated trading systems, which pushed down the price of SKYD stock. Skydance issued a press release Wednesday after market close noting that the warrants represent only around 9% of its Class B common stock. 

	According to Skydance, the implied value with the warrant distribution would have given Skydance a market cap of $45.6 billion at the $9.07/share price of the Class B stock — and that the value of the warrants at $2.20 each was around $1 billion (for total equity value of $46.6 billion). With the stock drop Wednesday, the market cap was around $36 billion. On Thursday, Skydance stock rebounded slightly, closing up 2.8% to $7.26, bringing the company’s market cap to $36.6 billion (not including the value of warrants, which had a closing price Thursday of $2.96 each).
	

	But beyond the disruption from the issuance of the stock warrants, there’s skepticism among analysts and credit-rating agencies that Skydance can hit the numbers the company’s top brass have projected. Ellison and his team will have to prove to Wall Street that they can achieve the $6 billion cost savings (on an annualized basis over the next three years) while continuing to invest in content — including more than 30 films released theatrically per year — and the rest of the business. All the while, Skydance will have to pay down its massive debt load. As it currently stands, the company’s interest payments alone will be north of $6 billion per year.

	With the merger’s closing, Paramount paid WBD shareholders an amount in cash equal to $31.01666668 per share for a total of about $78 billion. Under the terms of the deal, Paramount also is assuming WBD’s debt ($33.1 billion as of the end of June), leaving the merged company’s net debt at nearly $80 billion.

	Meanwhile, Skydance’s Class B investors don’t have a say in corporate governance issues. The Ellison family and RedBird Capital Partners are the sole holders of Skydance’s Class A stock, giving them 100% control the voting shares. (Those Class A shares do not have intrinsic value but have the option to for each share to be converted into 1.5 Class B shares, according to a Skydance SEC filing.)

	Some market watchers see a Skydance as an attractive investment opportunity after Wednesday’s stock drop.

	“There could be a buying opportunity in Skydance stock because the company’s share count hasn’t changed much with the warrant issuance” and “Skydance’s outlook hasn’t changed,” Barron’s associate editor Andrew Bary wrote in an Oct. 14 article. While the warrants, with the $12/share price, are currently underwater, they have value based on option pricing models “due to the long maturity of 10 years and the possibility that Skydance stock will rally in the coming years,” Bary added.

schema.headline: Skydance’s Market Value Is Currently Less Than Half What Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Combined Were Worth

title: Fandango Orders ‘Bad Girls Club: Unfinished Business’ as the Versant-Owned Streamer Gets Into Original Programming
description: Fandango, which became part of Versant Media when NBCUniversal split off most of its cable and digital offerings at the start of the year, is getti
body:
Fandango, which became part of Versant Media when NBCUniversal split off most of its cable and digital offerings at the start of the year, is getting into the original programming business — starting with a revival of “Bad Girls Club.”

	As part of Fandango’s AVOD streaming platform, the service has ordered two episodes of the unscripted special “Bad Girls Club: Unfinished Business.” “Bad Girls” vet Tanisha Thomas is set to host.
	

	Several “Bad Girls” stars from Season 7 — which Fandango said is the most-watched season of the series available on its service — will be included in the reunion. Among those participating: Stasi Townsend, Shelly Hickman, Judi Jackson, Tiara Hodge, Angie Castillo and Priscilla Mennella. They’ll be split into groups of three for each episode.


	“As we continue to evolve Fandango’s free, ad-supported streaming service, we want to deliver programming that fans are passionate about, and Bad Girls Club has consistently over-indexed with our viewers,” said Versant entertainment president Val Boreland in a statement. “We are thrilled to reunite fans with these unforgettable women and take longtime viewers back through the moments that made the franchise iconic.”

	“Bad Girls Club” originally ran for 17 seasons on Oxygen, from 2006 to 2017. It also spawned several spinoffs: “Bad Girls Road Trip,” “Tanisha Gets Married,” “Love Game: Bad Girls Need Love Too” and “Bad Girls All-Star Battle.” The final season was dubbed “Bad Girls Club: East Meets West.” After that, the show was displaced when Oxygen morphed into a true-crime cable outlet.
	

	According to Versant, the special will include memories of the original show, and its “most iconic fights and confrontations. Each episode brings the women face-to-face to share their sides of the story and unpack what really happened. With years of life experience between them, the Bad Girls will confront old tensions and determine if these chapters can finally be closed, or if some rivalries are simply too deep to leave in the past.”

	Bunim/Murray Productions, part of Banijay Entertainment, will produce the special (having been the company behind the original as well). Julie Pizzi, Steve Ezell, Brad Tiemann and Tanisha Thomas are executive producers.

schema.headline: Fandango Orders ‘Bad Girls Club: Unfinished Business’ as the Versant-Owned Streamer Gets Into Original Programming

title: The Most Shocking Thing About ‘You Can See Everything’: Nathan Fielder’s Sympathy for the Devil
description: Ever since the first trailer went up for “You Can See Everything,” if not since word of the movie got up, schadenfreude lovers have been rubbing th
body:
Ever since the first trailer went up for “You Can See Everything,” if not since word of the movie got up, schadenfreude lovers have been rubbing their hands with glee at the prospect of Elizabeth Holmes getting more of what’s coming to her. Especially knowing that Holmes and her husband Billy Evans actually sought out Nathan Fielder, who exudes a natural skepticism, to make the documentary, there’s been an anticipatory bloodlust, that they must have been fools to imagine they were doing anything but helping set their own trap. That’s not a completely ill-founded expectation: Holmes comes off in the doc as every bit as innately bizarre as anyone showing up for a cinematic freak show might hope. But the weirdest thing about the movie might be the fact that it at least allows for the possibility that the Evil Genius might be neither of the things contained in that descriptor, but rather somebody whose guileless act may not be that much of a put-on, because she’s dealing with some kind of mysterious damage we can only begin to guess at.
	

	In other words, it’s a movie with some sympathy for the devil, or at least — given the admitted inconclusiveness of its findings — the suggestion that empathy may be possible. Which may be not what you’re expecting walking in to what looks like a hilarious 174-minute takedown. But the intentions of Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim, are embedded right in that first trailer that set the watching world ablaze. At the scene’s very end, when after a couple of minutes of Holmes smiling and staring earnestly into the narrator’s eyes, with a shaky head that makes it appear as if she’s developed some kind of anxious palsy, it’s revealed that she’s extending her left leg well off the couch to rock her baby. If you were watching that teaser carefully, the filmmakers were carefully signaling the whole movie: vast amounts of IRL comedic shock and awe, tinged with lingering bits of poignance as Holmes turns out to be a human being… if a still-unfathomable one.
	

	So, let’s set a countdown for how long it takes for some souls on social media to begin calling Fielder a “cuck,” for having fallen prey to the manipulation of an obvious villain. But it’s not a movie that means to let Holmes off any hooks, only to ask some questions about where some of the invisible hooks in her impossibly strange life might lie. It’s a film that starts off with the intent to provide insight into a Leonard Nimoy-style Unsolved Mystery, with the idea that spending 34 days living with Holmes and Evans — and years of further production beyond her incarceration — would surely have to provide a few concrete conclusions about her psychology and/or crimes. Instead, by the end, it makes solving the puzzle of UFOs seem like a cinch by comparison. Abormal psychology: it’s the Ultimate Trip! But the idea that, amid that inability to form answers, we could at least further consider what makes her tick will seem risible and outrageous to some viewers… and is also what makes the film rich and re-visitable enough to deserve the Best Picture nomination it’s clearly lined up to get.

	If there’s a great crux moment for the movie, it’s in the scene fairly late in the three-hour proceedings that involve a sort of postmortem between Fielder and the Very Famous A-List Personality whose appearance A24 has asked viewers to consider a spoiler. (Her name will be ubiquitous enough in the weeks to come, but we can honor the surprise for now.) Fielder confesses how confused he is, after spending months doing intensive filming of Holmes and her husband and immediate family — basically wondering if, against all odds, it is possible that she could be as guileless as she comes off 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Upon hearing that confession, the Very Famous A-List Personality does everything but literally slap Fielder, suggesting that he must be experiencing some kind of Stockholm Syndrome to have been pulled in by her act. At this, some filmgoers will be practically standing up and cheering for the A-lister — she has at that moment become the audience’s surrogate, or stand-in for at least part of it, urging the host/filmmaker to snap out of his delirium. But it won’t just be different viewers taking sides in this scene. It may be anyone watching the movie whose empathic and cynical sides are in roughly equal balance.
	

	Where Fielder ultimately ended up on the issue of how sincere or Machiavellian Holmes is another unsolved mystery at the end of the movie, perhaps even to himself. When I caught the film at its Telluride Film Festival premiere (followed by a Q&A attendees weren’t allowed to record), Fielder basically said that he and others on the filmmaking team still had trouble figuring out exactly what they’d experienced in the process of making the movie — which is a fascinating conundrum, considering that, true to its title, Holmes and her husband did let them see just about everything it seemed possible to see. My personal hunch is that Fielder came away thinking Holmes is on the level, to the extent that someone who sometimes seems like an AI program’s idea of how a human should behave can be on the level. There are a few possibilities that might explain how Holmes comes off the way she does in the movie: (a) She is a simpleton. (b) She is a conniving sociopath who happens to be utterly brilliant at playing a simpleton. (c) Somewhere between those poles, she is the very emblem of a woman who throughout her life has put herself in the sway of controlling men, to the detriment of her intellect, willpower and emotional development.

	And what about those impossibly wide, unblinking eyes, and that gentle Joker smile? Are these the hallmarks, as I’ve seen theorized throughout the internet, of someone who is deeply sociopathic at worst, or on the scale at best? Or just someone with Resting Beatific Face?

	The sort of feminist lens is a powerful one, if you choose to go down that path of interpretation. Fielder and Oppenheim include a moment early in the film in which Holmes’ father blurts out that he believes things really started to change for his daughter when she was raped in her college days. On-camera, Fielder offers one of the quietly startled reaction shots that are a staple of the movie, and the topic never comes up again. The theme of her becoming the victim of powerful men continues — a little bit when the subject of Theranos co-founder Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani comes up (although recounting past history doesn’t take up much of this doc’s running time), and a lot when we get to the present day. Evans is as close as “You Can See Everything” has to a villain, and probably crosses the line into counting as one. Even he is treated as a rounded human being over the course of the film; he’s too candid and open about is intentions to count as a top-level devil, and it seems like he might actually love Holmes. But the succession of constant revelations about what he’s up to in the last hour of the movie make Holmes feel like a woman with virtually no personal agency, even before she goes to jail, let alone afterward, when he is making deals without her knowledge and keeping up a cocky, profane tweetstorm under her name that bears scant resemblance to her personality as we know it.
	

	It may be not giving Holmes nearly enough credit for her misdeeds to suggest that she has actually spent most of her adult years as a puppet. Yet the portrait of her passivity in the face of an aggressive “let me handle everything” man never stops growing more startling as the film goes on… and has to feels at least a little real for anyone with much first-hand human-race experience.

	Two scenes that explore Holmes’ seeming — and shocking — naivete stand out. (Neither of these count as major “plot” spoilers.) One comes early on when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied, and when she says no, he asks the inevitable what-about-white-lies question. Even then, it’s a no, as Fielder almost begs her to admit that she understands the question and has told a fib or two to protect a friend’s feelings. Probably 99.99% of the population would surrender at the point — evil geniuses most of all — but Holmes can’t admit to even having falsely complimented a pal. Later on, there’s a mind-blowing scene in which Fielder uses the historically famous Abbott and Costello “Who’s on first?” sketch as a setup to explore how people’s communication paths might just blow right by each other. Holmes hasn’t heard of the skit, but after watching it, she says she sees what he’s trying to say… which itself turns out to be a white lie, because she finally admits that she just doesn’t get what’s going on between Abbott and Costello, at all. And it’s at this point that you might start to wonder if she is just developmentally disabled in some way.

	Stunted in her growth, somehow, yet capable of convincing smart people to part with billions of dollars? Something here does not compute. And yet, intuitively, Holmes does not come off in this movie as someone with the kind of intellectual cunning to pretend not to understand an Abbott and Costello sketch that has entertained millions, or to not know what a white lie is. The enigma deepens.

	But so does the possibility that, for all her sins, and for all her Stanford education, Holmes is a simple gal — not simpleton — suffering from an extreme case of not just serial male dominance but terminal Imposters’ Syndrome. (Which is something that, from the available evidence in the movie, she surely would not admit to, not least of all because she might never have heard of it.)
	

	How people feel about Holmes after watching “You Can See Everything” might be the most divisive thing in America since… well, since Kelly Clarkson versus the Brooklyn boutique, the thing that has truly riven us as a nation. But one thing is clear: In this era of ever-shortening quick hits and hot takes, Fielder and Oppenheim’s luxuriously paced peering into someone’s soul feels like a balm, inconclusive or not. Is it possible that the more you learn about someone, the less you might know how to think about them?

	To take a cue from Shakespeare: “You Can See Everything” suggests that there are more things in the heaven and earth that is just one person than are dreamt of in any of our philosophies. We could do worse than to have the possibility of sympathy thrown in amid those hours of head-scratching assessment.

	(By the way, who is on first…)

schema.headline: The Most Shocking Thing About ‘You Can See Everything’: Nathan Fielder’s Sympathy for the Devil

title: Netflix Shocker: Bela Bajaria Leaving After 10 Years Amid Layoffs, Peter Rice to Replace as Chief Content Officer
description: In a major executive shake-up, Bela Bajaria is out at Netflix after 10 years at the streamer, most recently serving as its chief content officer.
body:
In a major executive shake-up, Bela Bajaria is out at Netflix after 10 years at the streamer, most recently serving as its chief content officer.

	She will be replaced by former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice, as first reported by Puck. As chief content officer, Rice will lead Netflix’s global content organization, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more across all regions.


	Bajaria’s exit comes amid a significant workforce reduction at Netflix. Around 1,000 employees (6% of the company) were laid off this week in what marks the streamer’s largest axing to date. Netflix’s film VP Doug Belgrad and film director Sheroum Kim were also pink slipped as part of the restructuring.
	

	“I want to thank Bela for a decade of dedication, innovation, creativity and leadership,” Sarandos, Netflix’s co-CEO, said in a statement. “She led enormous changes at Netflix. She helped broaden our content offering to include the large-scale expansion of unscripted programming and the launches of live events and sports, in addition to crafting and running a world class, global slate of films and series. I’m incredibly grateful for everything she’s done to help Netflix entertain the world.”

	Bajaria joined Netflix in 2016 after she was let go from NBCUniversal, where she had served as president of Universal Television. In that role, she had produced shows that aired on Netflix, including “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt” and “Master of None.” Sarandos first brought in Bajaria to help Netflix launch an unscripted division, as well as licensing and studio co-productions. Bajaria was later elevated to head of global in 2020 as Cindy Holland exited the company, and was named chief content officer in January 2023.
	

	Under her watch, Bajaria oversaw popular TV series including “Bridgerton,” “Squid Game,” “Adolescence,” “Beef,” “Stranger Things” and “Wednesday,” and films such as “KPop Demon Hunters” and “Frankenstein.” She also pushed Netflix into more live sports and events like “The Roast of Tom Brady” and deals with the NFL and WWE.

	But in recent months, as Netflix growth has slowed, so too has the aura around its original programming. The streamer won just 16 Primetime Emmy Awards this year — down from 30 in 2025 and quite a distance from 2021, when it tied the record for most Emmys won by an outlet in a single year, with 44. All told, 2026 was Netflix’s lowest Primetime Emmy haul since 2016.

	“I know this is a big change in a year that has already had its share,” Sarandos wrote in a memo to staff. “But I also see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in UCAN [United States and Canada] where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world.

	Rice’s own ousting at Disney in 2022, by then-CEO Bob Chapek, was a huge shock to the industry given his stature at the company. A well-regarded executive with strong talent relations, Rice was most recently chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the Walt Disney Company. There he oversaw ABC, FOX Broadcasting, Fox Sports, ABC News, ABC Studios, Disney Channel, Freeform, FX Networks, Hulu, National Geographic, Onyx Collective, Disney Television and Twentieth Century Fox Television, with more than 300 shows and 4,000 hours of television a year. Programs during his tenure included “The Simpsons,” “American Idol,” “Modern Family,” “This Is Us,” “The Bear,” “Abbott Elementary,” “Shogun” and “Only Murders in the Building,” along with ABC News programming and sporting events such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup Finals. 

	Since he was let go from Disney, Rice worked as a producer on movies such as Jason Reitman’s “Saturday Night,” “28 Years Later” and “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” at Sony, as well as “Warfare” and Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” at A24. He is currently producing Alex Garland’s “Elden Ring” and Sonoya Mizuno’s “Stages,” as well as well as the opening and closing ceremonies for the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
	

	Earlier in his career, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group, and Fox’s lead executive on the Hulu board. He also headed Fox Searchlight Pictures where he shepherded indie favorites like “Slumdog Millionaire,” “Juno,” “Little Miss Sunshine” and “Sideways.”

	“Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across TV and film is deep and broad,” Sarandos said. “He understands what makes stories resonate, and he’s spent his career helping talent do the best work of their lives. I’m excited to welcome him to Netflix as chief content officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love.”

	Added Rice, “Netflix has fundamentally changed the way stories are made, shared and experienced around the world. They’ve shown again and again that they’re willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I’m excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere.”

	Mike Schneider contributed to this report.

title: With ‘Obsession,’ Is the Golden Globes’ Comedy Race the New Home for Category Fraud?
description:
“Category fraud” is having a crossover moment.

	It happens every year, in awards cycles for both film and television. Campaigners submit films, sh
body:
“Category fraud” is having a crossover moment.

	It happens every year, in awards cycles for both film and television. Campaigners submit films, shows and individual performances in categories they have no business being in, like a drama masquerading as a comedy or a blatant leading role being tipped for a supporting category. Industry reactions to some of these bold decisions, however, feel louder this year.


	This creative maneuvering with category submissions happens for a reason: to improve the perceived odds of winning a trophy. Yet increasingly, the misrepresentations are spilling into broader industry discourse. (Just Google the limited series “The Beast in Me,” which was greenlit for a second season and Emmy winner Matthew Rhys.)
	

	This year, these so-called crimes seem to be targeting comedy categories. Curry Barker’s “Obsession,” made for $750,000 and now surpassing $500 million worldwide, was submitted by Focus Features as a musical or comedy for the Golden Globes, putting breakout star Inde Navarrette in the comedy actress race. Yes, there are laughs. But by and large, audiences were exposed to the horrors of a woman robbed of control over her own mind and body.

	Not long after, Bleecker Street submitted Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care” in the same comedy categories. Barely anyone blinked, perhaps because so few have seen it yet. The film features drunken sing-alongs and dancing with abandon in the family kitchen. It also features hospital visits and aging parents coming to terms with the final chapters of life. Hardly a laughing matter for anyone who has seen their loved ones slow down.
	

	A chuckle does not equate to comedy. The strategists know it, and so do the Globes. What’s missing is the nerve to define it and, more importantly, enforce it. This dilemma isn’t new. A decade ago, Ridley Scott’s “The Martian” won the Golden Globe for best motion picture comedy. You know, the one about a man stranded on Mars, trying not to starve to death. LOL! Wonder if the Globes will remember that when Amazon MGM’s “Project Hail Mary” comes calling, with Ryan Gosling and an adorable alien rock each trying to save their civilizations.

	Universal entered “Get Out” as a comedy in 2017 and got away with it. Focus tried it in 2020 with “Promising Young Woman,” about a woman avenging a friend’s assault. That time, voters said no and moved it to drama.

	The current Globes rulebook states a movie “primarily intended to have a serious or dramatic tone” with “comedic overtones or elements” belongs in drama.

	The Globes don’t account for intent, but they make all decisions using their “sole discretion” and their final rulings don’t come with an appeals process.

	When a submission is called into question, a committee assembled by the Golden Globes reviews the case and rules on potential disputes, whether they involve genre classification or lead-versus-supporting campaigns. Some strategists, anticipating that the committee may raise flags, now try to get ahead of the process by submitting additional documentation, including filmmaker quotes and source materials, to explain why a film belongs in its intended category.

	One top awards campaigner says that despite the attempts, the truth usually wins out.

	“You have to be up front and honest with your filmmakers,” says one awards strategist. “It’s about what sets up the movie for success overall. And if you think both classifications are too competitive, ‘frauding’ your movie doesn’t make it easier. The opposite will happen.”

	Musicals can be just as tricky to classify. “Ray” and “Walk the Line” competed in the Globes’ musical or comedy category. Still, in recent years, the organization has emphasized that songs must propel the story forward, rather than appear as performances, to qualify. That distinction sent “Bohemian Rhapsody” and “Elvis” to the drama category. By that standard, “Michael”’s classification remains an open question. Jaafar Jackson performs many of Michael Jackson’s biggest hits in the biopic, but whether those musical sequences are integral to the storytelling or simply re-creations of the King of Pop’s performances could determine where the film lands.
	

	The Globes could revisit their rules, but any awards campaigner will tell you: There’s always a way to moonwalk around them.

title: Taylor Sheridan’s ‘Frisco King’ Starring Samuel L. Jackson Sets Release Date (TV News Roundup)
description: Samuel L. Jackson is the new returning king in town in Taylor Sheridan’s “Frisco King,” where he reprises his role of Russell Lee Washington Jr..
body:
Samuel L. Jackson is the new returning king in town in Taylor Sheridan’s “Frisco King,” where he reprises his role of Russell Lee Washington Jr..

	The New Orleans gangster establishes a new kingdom in Frisco, Texas, where he discovers a hustler running his business amid the suburban town. Per the series logline, “Recruiting an ambitious protégé, a loyal driver and a growing network of eccentric partners, Lee transforms small hustles into big business. But, every new score raises the stakes, and as his influence grows, so do the risks, forcing Lee to stay one grift ahead. Frisco may not know it yet, but its new king has arrived.”
	

	The series will premiere on Paramount+ Dec. 18 with two episodes, followed by new episodes weekly. Starring alongside Jackson are Asa Germann, Kai Caster, Lilah Pate and Savanna Gann, with a special appearance by Sylvester Stallone.


	Written by Sheridan, “Frisco King” is executive produced by Stallone, Jackson, Sheridan, David C. Glasser, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, LaTanya Richardson Jackson and Keith Cox. Christina Alexandra Voros and Michael Friedman executive produce in addition to both directing four episodes, with Voros directing the pilot. The series is produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios,

	Watch the teaser for “Frisco King” below.



	In other TV roundup news:
	
		Specials	

	CBS set “The Price is Right at Night: Live Holiday Special” and “The Price is Right: 20 Seasons of Drew Carey” to air in December.

	“The Price is Right at Night: Live Holiday Special” will premiere on Dec. 13 at 8 p.m. ET on CBS. The broadcast marks the first time television’s longest-running game show will air in real time. Viewers will also get behind-the-scenes access with host Drew Carey, announcer George Gray, the models and the production team as they race to keep the show on track.
	

	On Dec. 15, CBS will air “The Price is Right: 20 Seasons of Drew Carey.” The special will celebrate two decades of Carey as host, featuring celebrity appearances from previous episodes including Mila Kunis, Jack Black and Snoop Dogg.

	The live holiday special is produced by Fremantle, with John Quinn as showrunner and executive producer. The Drew Carey special is produced by Fremantle, with James Davis and Quinn as executive producers. Both specials will be available to stream on Paramount+.
	
		Initiatives	

	FilAm Creative announced its inaugural TV Creator Lab cohort of 25 writers.

	The tuition-free, five-month program is designed to help emerging television creators develop their original scripted series. The selected writers will learn from working television executives, producers, showrunners and industry professionals.

	The Lab launched Oct. 8 at Patriot Pictures in Los Angeles. The cohort gathered for a conversation with Lionsgate SVP of Television Richard Rothschild, Greg Coolidge (“The Continental: From the World of John Wick”) and Oren Segal, moderated by television director Francis dela Torre (“Almost Paradise”).

	The writers selected are Angel Cielo, Candice Sarangay, Celena Cipriaso, Eileen Cabiling, Ella Espiritu, Eric J. De La Rosa, Eugene Ramos, Faith Christy Soliven, Frances Rubio, Geri Carillo, Hermie Castillo, Jaime Estepa, Jalen Giovanni Jones, Joshua Labata, Joy Regullano, Kim Marcelino, Nicole Wolf, Noël Wiggins, Rebecca Williams Spindler, Roann Enriquez, Rommel Rojas, Stacie Gancayco-Adlao, Teodorico Sajor, Walter Boholst and Yasmine Gomez.

	*

	The American Film Institute announced the mentors for its 2026 Writers’ Room Ready program.

	This year’s mentors are Brad Ingelsby (“Task,” “Mare of Easttown”), Peter Gould (“Better Call Saul,” “Breaking Bad”) Patrik-Ian Polk (“Noah’s Arc,” “P-Valley”), Sev Ohanian (“Sinners,” “Searching”) and Sarah-Violet Bliss (“Scorn,” “Search Party”).

	The creatives will be paired with AFI Class of 2025 graduates:Brad Ingelsby with Nathan Bouton — “Black Tide,” one-hour dramaPeter Gould with Kirby Saxton — “Holy Water,” half-hour comedyPatrik-Ian Polk with Chri’shawn Julius — “Pop Puss,” half-hour comedySev Ohanian with Edward Nenedzhyan — “The Optic,” one-hour dramaSarah-Violet Bliss with Annabel Newland — “Glitter,” half-hour comedy
	

	“Great writing is taught in community, not isolation,” said Susan Ruskin, AFI Conservatory dean and executive vice president of the American Film Institute. “We are deeply grateful to our accomplished mentors, whose wisdom, expertise and generosity empower our Writers’ Room Ready participants to transform their potential into professional practice in the industry.”

	The Writers’ Room Ready program recognizes outstanding original television pilot scripts written by AFI Conservatory Screenwriting Fellows.
	
		Partnerships 	

	Elmo and his “Sesame Street” friends are taking on an African safari adventure in a special PBS ‘Nature’ primetime crossover. “Sesame Street and the Great Elephant Adventure” premieres on Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 8 p.m. ET on PBS and PBS Kids and will stream on pbs.org/nature, YouTube,pbskids.org, the PBS KIDS Video app and the PBS app.

	Per the release, “The adventure begins at the group’s safari lodge, where they meet the lodge manager and her young daughter, who introduce Elmo and Abby to Kenya’s culture, nature and wildlife. Along the way, Elmo struggles with the idea of leaving his adopted elephant behind but comes to learn that the greatest way to care for his new friend is to let her thrive where she belongs: in the wild.”

	“Bringing Elmo and the ‘Sesame Street’ friends into the world of ‘Nature’ allows us to tell a unique story filled with adventure, discovery, and heart,” Sal Perez, executive producer for Sesame Workshop, said. “We hope this special event sparks curiosity in children and encourages them to see themselves as explorers and problem solvers, while reminding viewers of every age that some of life’s greatest lessons come from experiencing nature.”
	
		Programming	

	Moonbug Entertainment announced that actress and performer Lauren Vaz will join Cashaé Monya in playing Meekah in the global “Blippi” franchise.

	“Lauren brings such a natural warmth, confidence and sense of fun to Meekah,” Liz Katz, Associate General Manager of “Blippi” and lead of the Meekah franchise, said. “She really captures the curiosity and big-sister energy that families know and love about Meekah. We’re so excited to welcome her to our ensemble cast alongside Cashaé Monya as we enter an exciting new chapter for Meekah, with more to share in the weeks ahead.”
	

	“Blippi” is a live-action kids’ franchise built around curiosity, exploration and real-world adventures. Meekah is an established character who can be brought to life by different performers. Vaz now joins Monya in sharing the role across the Blippi franchise, as Meekah prepares to enter an exciting new chapter.

	“Getting to step into Meekah’s shoes is incredibly special to me,” Vaz said. “I love how she encourages kids to be curious, express themselves and have the confidence to jump in and try something new. Having already been part of the Blippi world on tour, I’m so excited to continue this journey with Meekah and bring my personality, creativity and sense of fun to all the adventures ahead.”
	
		Executive News	

	Hearst Media Production Group named Amy DeGregorio as executive vice president of sales and revenue.

	In the newly created role, DeGregorio will act as a key member of HMPG’s executive team and strategic advisor to the company’s president on revenue growth, commercialization and new business opportunities. She will be responsible for driving revenue strategy and overseeing sales and sponsorship activity.

	Prior to her new role, DeGregorio served as senior vice president, managing director of sales for educational/informational programming for HMPG since 2022.

	“Amy has done an exceptional job building meaningful brand partnerships and seamlessly integrating sponsors into our E/I programming,” said Bryan Curb, HMPG president. “As HMPG continues to expand, we want to bring that same expertise and strategic approach to our entire portfolio, creating new opportunities for brands to engage with our award-winning content and loyal audiences.”

	In 2016, DeGregorio joined Litton Entertainment, which was rebranded to HMPG in 2022, as senior director, integrated marketing. She was promoted to vice president, integrated marketing and, in 2020, senior vice president, client solutions. Before joining Litton, she worked at CBS Television Stations, and has held roles at NBCUniversal, truTV, ABC Television and MTV Networks.

title: Katie Zacharia Says She Failed The Bar Exam Because She Was Distracted By Wedding Plans
description:
Katie Zacharia
                          I Failed The Bar Because I Was Distracted By Wedding Pla
body:
Katie Zacharia
                          I Failed The Bar Because I Was Distracted By Wedding Plans
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 15, 2026
                            1:58 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Katie Zacharia says her mind was elsewhere when she took the bar exam in California ... and she failed because she was too distracted by planning her wedding.
      
    
      
      Kate Zacharia tells Jack Posobiec that she was distracted when she took the bar exam because she had just gotten engaged, but it didn't matter anyway because passing it was "inconsequential" since she  "knew I wouldn’t need the bar in China."
When asked why she never took the bar again, she says it was because she started having kids, and it was "okay and acceptable" to label herself a "lawyer" for the work she was doing.
              @justinbaragona
          
  
    
            The new White House Press Secretary admitted Thursday that she never passed the bar despite presenting herself as a "lawyer" ... and she went with the wedding-planning excuse in an interview with Jack Posobiec on "Real America's Voice."
      
    
            Katie says she failed the bar in 2011 after graduating from Pepperdine University's law school ... claiming she was not only distracted by planning her wedding to Tyler Zacharia, but also by her plans to move to China to be with Tyler.
      
    
            Failing was no biggie ... Katie says it as "inconsecuential" because she "knew I wouldn't need the bar in China."
      
    
            When Katie moved to China, she worked on international transaction law at Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China’s biggest law firms,
      
    
            Katie was one-and-done with the bar ... when asked why she never tried again, she said it was because she started having kids. Katie and Tyler have four children.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Folks started digging into her legal background after Trump hired her as his new White House press secretary and promoted her as an "attorney."
      
    
            Katie's social media bio said she was a "lawyer," and she claims it was "okay and acceptable" to label herself a "lawyer" for the work she was doing ... despite not actually being one.
      
    
            She previously told TMZ ... "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
      
    
            A White House official told us ... Katie has her JD from Pepperdine. Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law.

title: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Used to Work for a 'Pyramid Scheme'
description:
Katie Zacharia
                          I Worked for a Pyramid Scheme!!!
body:
Katie Zacharia
                          I Worked for a Pyramid Scheme!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 15, 2026
                            12:35 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia may not have passed the bar ... but she did work for a multilevel marketing company.
      
    
            According to WIRED, Zacharia worked as an affiliate of the fitness company Beachbody, and she told the outlet the company ran a multilevel marketing structure that she says was "sort of a pyramid scheme."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The outlet used a database of leaked online material from District 4 Labs, which included Zacharia's since-deleted LinkedIn profile that displayed Beachbody email addresses as her points of contact.
      

            Both Beachbody and Zacharia confirmed she was never employed by the company, but she told WIRED she was an affiliate marketer, brought in by a friend promoting the Shakeology "superfood nutrition shake."
      
    
            She claims she eventually stopped using and promoting Shakeology because she didn't believe the vitamin A was good for her while she was pregnant.
      
    
            Beachbody has since rebranded as BODi ... and the company confirmed in a statement that Zacharia was one of their "independent Team Beachbody distributors."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            BODi tells WIRED in a statement ... "Team Beachbody was a peer-to-peer sales and support network ... helped tens of millions of people pursue their health goals through in home fitness programs like P90X, Insanity, and 21 Day Fix, and nutrition products such as Shakeology."
      
    
            Katie's "pyramid scheme" past comes amid a deep dive into her background. Trump claimed she was an "attorney," but the Wall Street Journal reports that she never actually passed the bar exam.

title: Former Six Flags Operator Explains How Goliath Restraint Could've Opened on Fatal Ride
description:
Six Flags Over Georgia Death
                          With Enough Force You Could Open Safety Re
body:
Six Flags Over Georgia Death
                          With Enough Force You Could Open Safety Restraint ...
                          Former Operator Claims
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 15, 2026
                            12:22 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 15, 2026
                                1:51 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            A former Six Flags Over Georgia operator says it's possible to push a restraint on a ride like Goliath open ... though it would take a tremendous amount of force.
      
    
            Brycen Whatley -- a former employee at the theme park near Atlanta and a roller coaster enthusiast -- joined us on "TMZ Live" Thursday to discuss how Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem might have been ejected from Goliath before falling to his death.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Brycen first ran through the safety measures on Goliath ... explaining the ride can't even move unless pin-and-gear arm restraints are pulled down three notches -- locking a person into place.
      

            However, Brycen mentions the possibility of pin-slipping ... a phenomenon where the components latched into place in the arm restraint come undone. He says this usually affects only one latch, if it happens at all -- adding that it's highly unlikely the whole thing would bust open.
      
    
            That said, Brycen admits that -- if a ton of force is applied to the restraint -- it could bust open. Again, unlikely ... but by no means impossible.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            To be clear ... Brycen doesn't work at the park anymore -- and he wasn't working when Hassan died, but he used to work on the ride and several others in the park.
      
    
            Investigators are still looking into the cause of Hassan's shocking death after he flew out of the car, slammed multiple times into the ride's tracks, and landed beneath the coaster.
      
    
            Bottom line ... roller coasters are built with a ton of safety features -- but they're by no means perfectly safe.
